'''''Capparis sepiaria''''', also commonly called '''hedge caper''' or '''wild caper bush''', is a shrub that has a [[pantropical]] distribution, especially in dry deciduous forests, foothills and scrub jungles.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Capparis sepiaria L.|url=https://indiabiodiversity.org/species/show/32077|access-date=2021-06-29|website=India Biodiversity Portal}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Capparis sepiaria L. - Encyclopedia of Life|url=https://eol.org/pages/47120195|access-date=2021-06-29|website=eol.org}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Capparis sepiaria'' is a prickly, evergreen shrub growing to 3 to 5 meters tall, with white flowers during season. It flowers from February onwards, and fruits start developing in April.<ref name=":0" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Capparis sepiaria'' has a [[pantropical]] distribution, and has been found in [[Africa]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Myanmar]], [[India]], [[Australia]]. In India, it has been observed in [[Kolhapur]], [[Chikmagalur]], [[Dharwad]], [[Mysore]], [[Shimoga]], [[Hyderabad]] and various areas of [[Kerala]] and Tamil Nadu, including the [[Nilgiri Mountains]] in the [[Western Ghats]], where the locals, like the [[Irula people|Irulas]], are familiar with it for various traditional medicinal uses.<ref name=":0" />

== Ecological significance ==
In the areas where ''Capparis sepiaria'' grows in [[Rajasthan]], it appears to be an important source of [[fodder]] for local wildlife, like the [[chital]], [[Sambar deer|sambar]], and [[nilgai]], who like to eat the shoots.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rodgers|first=W.A.|date=1990|title=Capparis sepiaria L.: an important dry season fodder plant for wildlife.|url=https://www.cabdirect.org/cabdirect/abstract/19920755670|journal=Range Management and Agroforestry |volume=11|issue=2|pages=199–206|via=CAB Direct}}</ref> 

Like many members of the ''[[Capparis]]'' genus, various parts of the plant, especially the flowers and fruit, are used as food or traditional medicine.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sharma|first1=Leena|last2=Khandelwal|first2=Sitaram|date=2010-02-01|title=Traditional Uses of Plants as Cooling Agents by the Tribal and Traditional Communities of Dang Region in Rajasthan, India|url=https://opensiuc.lib.siu.edu/ebl/vol2010/iss2/9|journal=Ethnobotanical Leaflets|volume=2010|issue=2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=2004-10-01|title=Ethnomedicine of Dharwad district in Karnataka, India—plants used in oral health care|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S037887410400220X|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|language=en|volume=94|issue=2–3|pages=261–266|doi=10.1016/j.jep.2004.04.021|issn=0378-8741|last1=Hebbar|first1=S.S.|last2=Harsha|first2=V.H.|last3=Shripathi|first3=V.|last4=Hegde|first4=G.R.|pmid=15325728|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mishra|first1=S. N.|last2=Tomar|first2=P. C.|last3=Lakra|first3=N.|publication-date=January 2007|title=Medicinal and food value of Capparis—a harsh terrain plant|url=http://nopr.niscair.res.in/handle/123456789/911|journal=Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge |volume=6 |issue=1 |date=January 2007|language=en-US|issn=0972-5938}}</ref>  The flowers are pollinated by bees and the tree bark is an important larval host plant for the [[Hebomoia glaucippe|great orange-tipped butterfly]] and [[Ixias pyrene|yellow orange tip butterfly]] of South India.<ref name=":0" /><ref>Butterflies of Bengaluru, Forest Department of Karnataka, Page 54 & Page 64 (http://biodiversitylab.ncbs.res.in/media/ButterfliesOfBengaluruBook_Sample.pdf)</ref>
